utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and around the courtroom. Appearing for Mr. Perisic today are Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure by now you do know that you are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of the testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Prosecutor Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to finish your evidence this morning, and I'm sure you would like to finish your evidence this morning as well, so listen carefully to my questions and we will accomplish that task. On what date did the refugees from the Cazin area enter into Kordun and create a humanitarian crisis?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Mr. Harmon, that was on the 20th and 21st of August, 1994, the refugees came from the areas of Cazin and Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on what date did Operation Pauk begin?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Pauk, as far as I can remember, started in mid-December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 902 on the monitor, the first page of that exhibit in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can see that that copy in the Serbian language is a little difficult to read off the monitor. Do you have problems reading that, General? I have a hard copy for you if it is difficult for you to read.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is really hardly legible on the screen, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the assistance of the monitor and with the Court's permission could I give the witness a hard copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that better, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhat better, although --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but it's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not -- there is a copy for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will begin by identifying this document. First of all, this is a document from the Main Staff of the VRS that is dated the 2nd of July, 1994, and if we could go to the last page in the -- the second-to-last page in the English, page 3, I want to see the signature of the person who issued this combat order. Thank you. We can see it in English. If we go into the B/C/S -- or actually, that's fine. General, can you just look at the last page in the copy in front of you and tell us whose name appears to be the person who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the last page in the left bottom corner I see the words "Deputy Commander Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we return to the first page of the two versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, General, I want to direct your attention while you have the document in hand I'm going to be discussing the paragraph 2, so if you could get a head start and start reading that. All right. Paragraph 2 of this combat order reads that: "Pursuant to the agreement between the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of Republika Srpska, the Serbian Army of Krajina, and the armed forces of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, Directive 6 issued by the Supreme Command and the armed forces of Republika Srpska on 11 November 1993, and the agreement concluded in Vojnic on 24 June 1994 between the representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of Republika Srpska, the Army of Krajina, and the military representatives of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, the Army of Republika Srpska has the task of starting offensive operations on 10 July, 1994, in the direction of the River Una engaging as much as possible the forces of the 5th Corps of the so-called BH Army, reaching the right bank of the River Una, and thus making it possible to carry out the plans of the armed forces of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia for the full control of the territory of Cazin Krajina." Now, sir, let me ask you in respect of this document, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. This document at the beginning of paragraph 2 refers to an agreement between the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of the Republika Srpska, the Serbian Army of Krajina which you were the commander, and the armed forces of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia. It makes a reference to an agreement. What was that agreement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask that -- those who took part in reaching that agreement. At that time, I was not in the command structure of the SVK or the VRS or the VJ, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. But you were still in the SVK and you were still an advisor to -- you still held a high position in the army, did you not? So an agreement between the VJ, the SVK, the VRS, and the autonomous province of Western Bosnia would be something that would be quite important, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this document is entitled -- is dated the 2nd of July, 1994. I don't believe -- it's doubtful that at that time I was not in the SVK, neither in those other two aforementioned armies, nor was I in any way involved in preparing or reaching such an agreement, nor do I know anything about that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You say that you were not in the SVK on the 2nd of July, 1994? That's your testimony as translated.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At the time I was deputy supreme commander for national security and international relations, as I've stated on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you still hold a post in the SVK on the 2nd of July, 1994? Were you still a member of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I was assistant supreme commander for national security and international relations. If I were to say that I was involved in the SVK, then I would have to tell you what exact post I held in the SVK at the time. At the time I held no posts in the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's turn to the second part of this paragraph 2, and it references a meeting -- an agreement that was concluded on the 24th of June, 1994, in Vojnic. Vojnic is in the RSK, it's a town in the RSK, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you tell us anything about the -- an agreement that took place in the RSK involving the representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia, the Republika Srpska, the SVK, and the military representatives from the autonomous province of Western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina was General Celeketic and there was no love lost between us. What he took part I never took part in, which means that I wasn't there in Vojnic concerning what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. We can see, General, at the end of this second paragraph General Milovanovic says that the VRS is supposed to start offensive operations on the 10th of July in the direction of the River Una, and thus make it possible to carry out plans for Fikret Abdic's forces to take full control over the Cazin Krajina. Operation Pauk had similar objectives, that is, to take-over territory in the Cazin Krajina area, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Answering to your question about the similarities and differences between these operations and Operation Pauk would require plenty of time that you would deem unnecessary. In essence, those were operations against the 5th Corps in both cases; that much is correct. With this difference, the VRS before and after this operation and after what was deemed -- labelled as Operation Pauk did take action through its 2nd Krajina Corps against the 5th Corps in the Cazin region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, sir. I'm done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, in paragraph 7 of this document let's clarify matters for the benefit of the Bench. In sentence 1 it states: "Operation is to be carried out under the title Una-94." Does it present clearly that this is not Operation Pauk then, and in such a light I don't know what the gist of your questions are --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you for a minute. I never asserted that this was Operation Pauk. I was asking you if there were similarities in terms of the objectives between the Una operation and Operation Pauk. And I believe you answered that question for me, so we are concluded with this document. Now, what was Operation Breza 94?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear about an operation named Breza 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't know anything about it, we will conclude the topic and we'll move to another topic, General. What was the Pauk command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you are expecting me to say that I was commander of the Pauk command. I answer that I was commander of Pauk command for that part, referring to carrying out of combat operation; but I wasn't a commander with full authority of a commander as defined in the word "commander." And this needs an explanation if you'd like to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, my question -- we will get to that point. My question -- if you listen carefully to my question I asked you: What was the Pauk command? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pauk command comprised of Supreme Command of the People's Defence of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, Serif Mustedanagic was at the head of that, and four to five Serbian officers headed by me who assisted them in planning combat operations and in co-ordination of these combat operations with the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you have the role of the commander of the Pauk command or did you have the title of commander in the Pauk command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unclear to me what you mean - and I insist on it - what is the role and what is the title, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I corrected my question and I changed it from the role to the title. Were you -- did you issue orders under the title of commander of Pauk command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what is agreed upon by the representatives of the units taking part in specific action and if -- and agreed upon by Fikret Abdic as the president of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, on the basis of that I signed my name under the results of such agreements and joint consultations for specific combat activities and operations as a commander over the carrying out of such combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'll give you an opportunity to explain your role as opposed to your title. What was your actual role in the Pauk operation? You mentioned co-ordination. What forces were you co-ordinating?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I co-ordinated the use of those forces that I enumerated yesterday as taking part in operations during Operation Pauk, and if need be I may repeat those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, sir. In terms of the orders that you issued, did you issue combat orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued exclusively combat orders on the basis of decisions taken by representatives of all the units and all the amassed that were supposed to take part in such a combat activity or action or operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you prepare regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I prepare regular combat reports you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I asked you, sir, yes. Did you prepare regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular combat reports, no; but interim combat reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you send those combat reports that you prepared to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To whom did you send those combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, such combat reports we would send to the Main Staff of the SVK from time to time and State Security Service of Serbia, attention of Mr. Milosevic; and I may have informed the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia on what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you send regular combat reports and extraordinary combat reports to General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extraordinary reports, yes, but no regular reports as far as I can remember. I wanted to keep him posted of the situation. To be -- to use a precise military term, and this is an important distinction, those reports were information in their character and purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have XN321 on the monitor, please, and I am interested in 0 -- English translation 0280-6335, B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this point I want to refresh the witness's recollection with it if -- well, it's to impeach him, Your Honour, but I want to explore this with him, so that's the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's used for impeachment, I do not object for the document to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, the document in front of you is a regular combat report. It is dated the 3rd of May, 1995, and it bears a typed name, your name, at the bottom. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Mr. Harmon. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see a discrepancy in the translation, and you will see that for yourself. In the date on the original document -- I'm checking whether this is the same document, yes, it is. It says here 11th of May in the original and in the English translation is the 3rd of May, 1995. I only hope that this is the only problem with translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the wrong document in B/C/S, so that's the problem. The B/C/S version that I have says the 3rd of May, and perhaps I gave you the wrong page reference but I don't think so. 0280-6335, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you're sorting that out, Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- can we see the signed part in the English part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Registrar please go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, sir, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Novakovic, this has your typed name under the title of "commander." And we can see, if we can go -- at the top that this document emanates from the Pauk command. We can see that at the top of the document on the first page in the English, if we could return to the first page in the English. Now, sir, this was sent to -- personally to General Perisic. It doesn't say for information. It was sent to General Perisic, it was sent to the -- obviously to General Celeketic, to the commander of the 21st command, the 39th command, the 2nd Krajina Corps of the VRS, and it's a regular combat report. How often did you send these types of regular combat reports to General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the very list of people and their positions to whom this combat report was sent shows that the report was sent to persons who, apart from the Main Staff of the SVK, are not in a relationship of subordination. So that is there was no hierarchy in place with regard to the Pauk command. The Chief of General Staff of the VJ and the commander of the 21st Corps and the commander of the 39th Corps and the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps in the last line, seem to be at an equal rank, at an equal level --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute. My question to you was: How often did you send these types of regular combat reports to General Perisic? That was my question. Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was your question, I think it was about once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you send a regular combat report to General Perisic once a week?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I sent information about the situation to General Perisic for the same reason as to the commander of the 2nd Corps, the commander of the 21st Corps of the SVK, and the commander of the 39th Corps of the SVK, and that is for them to be familiar with the development of the situation and the circumstances in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You also sent a request to General Perisic to provide you and your operation with logistical assistance and materiel, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when the Main Staff of the SVK couldn't provide or Mr. Fikret Abdic in the ways that he had available, the ways and means he had available, but I'm not familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Pauk operation consume large amounts of ammunition, for example, artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would sooner say that the consumption was normal, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. The Pauk operation you told us began in December of 1994 and it ended in August of 1995, so there must have been a fairly large consumption of ammunition, small arms ammunition, and artillery ammunition. Would you agree with me or not agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all militaries of the world, there are standards, Mr. Harmon, standards with regards to ammunition consumption. Sometimes the unit of measure is a day of warfare. So you can apply the standard to establish how much ammunition will be required. If we were to apply NATO standards, then the consumption was small.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So tell me, what was the volume of small arms ammunition you consumed in Operation Pauk, using the standards that you have described ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I cannot tell you off the top of my head. I don't want to mention a ballpark figure and then it can turn out to be wrong. It's the logistics officers who can say more about that, but there are international standards, and I can -- and I'm speaking on the basis of what I heard as going on on the front line. But I never dealt with the figures and tables and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- are you able to recall how many times you went to General Perisic or sent requests to General Perisic for logistical support for Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it happened at least once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I won't pursue the matter further, General. Let me ask you as the Pauk commander, sir, did you maintain a Pauk command operations log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, in the BH press after the war I saw a -- I saw the copy of such a log-book. I believe that it was kept for a while. Whether it was kept all the time or not, I don't know. It was kept, I suppose, by the officer in the operations room. But I repeat that I saw entries from that log-book after the war in the BH media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I tender XN321 into evidence, please, could it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It shall be given Exhibit P02927. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, isn't it standard operating procedure in the military when there is an operation -- military operation being conducted to maintain a log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a standard army and in a standard command, certainly, Mr. Harmon; that is one of the basic standards. But this was not a permanent formation nor an establishment unit, nor was it indeed a true command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So what you can tell us -- actually, let me take that back. When an operations log-book is maintained, what is the purpose of maintaining a log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the log-book is for all messages to be recorded in the form it was received. It is not for the one entering it to interpret it or to assess its credibility, but simply to make a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the note includes the person who communicated to the operations room and -- correct? So the person who sent the message or sent the order or transmitted a communication is recorded in an operations log-book; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The participants to a communication must be entered and the nature of the communication, whether it's a report, an order, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a communications log-book kept at the forward command post for Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny that. I didn't go to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, when a log-book -- a log-book is issued and items are recorded in it and you get to the last page of a log-book, is it supposed to -- is there supposed to be an official closing of that book with the signature from someone who will certify that the book has -- is an official book?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And who in the Pauk command would be the person who would execute that procedure? Who would sign at the end of a log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're speaking about the communications station, then it would be the chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And what role did Cedo Bulat have in the Pauk command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Colonel Cedomir Bulat was Chief of Staff in that Serbian component of the Pauk command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what role, if any, he would have with the Pauk command log-book in terms of its maintenance or in terms of its -- yeah, in terms of its maintenance and possession?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he must have been the person who organised the work of our component of the command and who took care of the functioning of that component, and the other component was the People's Defence of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, during a military operation various participants have code-names or call-signs; that's standard operating procedure, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your code-name in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Pauk, Spider.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of Operation Pauk, sir, were there battle groups?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some combat assignments, battle groups were established. Whether or not they were established depended on the purpose of the manoeuvre --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters didn't hear the last part of your answer. Could you please repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battle groups were established because they were not establishment units. Battle groups of different strength and different composition were formed for various assignments or for various phases of the carrying out of combat missions. Their composition was not permanent; it changed. So the answer is: Yes, they were formed occasionally, but they were temporary units, temporary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what are tactical groups? Is there a difference between a battle group and a tactical group?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference in principle between a battle group and a tactical group. Battle groups should be around about a battalion strong or a reinforced battalion, whereas tactical groups are usually a brigade plus something in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you remember -- you said essentially that these battle groups -- I mean the tactical groups and battle groups are essentially ad hoc. Depends on the situation. They were formed for particular assignments. Did I understand your evidence properly?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, and their composition varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday at the end of your evidence I had asked you which groups had participated in Operation Pauk, and you identified some groups for me. And then you said nothing else came to mind. Maybe I could jog your memory and you could remember. So let me try to jog your memory. I want to show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have XN393 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to see if the witness -- I may not introduce this document. I want to show the witness this document; it may assist him in remembering who certain people are and what their roles are. I'm not seeking its introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't asked him about any people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, if I am permitted to show him XN393, I intend to ask him about the people who appear in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a problem with such a question being asked, but if Mr. Harmon were to tender this particular photograph then he would have to state a reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me direct your attention in this exhibit to the person on the left of the image. Can you identify that person?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I can not only identify the persons in this photograph, I can also tell you where the place -- I can tell you the place where it was taken and the time is -- can be seen in the photograph anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's start with identifying the person on the left. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Milorad Ulemek, also known as Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you said you could identify both persons. Who's the person then in the centre of this image holding the binoculars?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Slobodan Medic, who at that time was the commander of a unit that had arrived from the eastern part, the 11th Corps. It only -- it was only supposed to stay for a limited time and it never saw combat. If you wish, I can tell you where exactly this photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please, General. Where was it taken?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken at Gladno Brdo, 700 metres from the place where -- when this photograph was taken, my electronic surveillance unit discovered a Hamze Mujahedin group established by Bin Laden. We opened fire and reduced their strength from 12 to 8. That is why I exactly remember the place and time when this photograph was taken. Whether or not Bin Laden was there at the time, perhaps -- I don't know. But he may have been in Mr. Izetbegovic's office, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We won't explore that possibility, General, but you were present when this photograph was taken, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've just said that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this image was taken from a film. Have you seen the film from which this image was taken?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, several times. It was broadcast several times on Serbian television channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let us start with the man on the left, Legija. What unit -- first of all, what role did he have in the Pauk operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while he was an advisor in the 2nd Brigade during Operation Pauk, the 2nd Brigade of the People's Defence of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, and the commander's name was Zumret, I forget his last name. Later when some other units of company level were added to that brigade, he was the commander of the tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was the commander of Tactical Group 2, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Tactical Group 2 come under your command, your specific command or did it come under someone else's command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the agreement was reached and the decision was taken to launch a particular combat operation, then he too, like other unit commanders of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, were under my technological command for the carrying out of that combat operation. But when it wasn't about the carrying out of a combat operation the units of Western Bosnia were not under my command nor were they units of the SVK or any other units under my command. It even happened that we -- once we planned a certain combat mission and a planned participant wouldn't take part in the implementation, then it wouldn't be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the Pauk operation, what unit did he come from?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are you asking me about, sir, Mr. Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the man in the far left of the photograph, Legija. Before Operation Pauk started he was in a military formation. Can you tell us what military formation he was in?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know which military formation he was in. You just used his nickname to refer to him, Legija, whereas I called him by his real name, Ulemek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Ulemek was a member of a paramilitary formation known as the Serb Volunteer Guard, wasn't he? He was a member of Arkan's Tigers before he came to Operation Pauk; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Mr. Ulemek was a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in February 1993, that is correct; but outside that period and all the time until Operation Pauk is something I cannot possibly know. But I know for certain that he was in February 1993 because I saw him on -- that unit came to help us after the Croatian offensive in Ravni Kotari in Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how many members of Arkan's Tigers came with Mr. Ulemek to assist in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I had no way of finding out who belongs to the Tigers or anybody else. I saw five or six men around Mr. Ulemek. Whether there were others who belonged there or elsewhere, I had no possibility to find out nor did I have the desire to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why didn't you have the desire to do so? You were the commander of Operation -- of Operation Pauk. Why didn't you have a desire to find out what units within your available forces came from?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I was interested in the strength of those units and the problems with the use of those units in combat. I had no time to check their IDs. I didn't even have the right to check the files of any member of the SVK to see which unit they belonged to. Whoever was sent there simply arrived and that there was no -- it wouldn't have been logical for me to line them up and then check who belonged to which unit and where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who sent Mr. Ulemek to Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you travel to Belgrade with Mr. Ulemek while you were commander of Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how long were you in Belgrade with Mr. Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Belgrade with Mr. Ulemek. I was there on my own without his company. As far as I understood, he had some burning political problems, whereas I had my own activities there. I believe that my stay there lasted for a day or two and I even think that he didn't return with us after that spell in Belgrade -- no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember when you travelled to Belgrade with Mr. Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was sometime at the beginning of 1995, Mr. Harmon, but I cannot specify the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Who summoned you to Belgrade with Legija, with Mr. Ulemek?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to go to visit Mr. Milosevic then, and I think that Mr. Ulemek was supposed to meet Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when Mr. Ulemek was the commander of Tactical Group 2, how many men were under his command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was approximately 1200, maybe at times 1500, men or maybe I would be exaggerating. Slightly above 1.000 men at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Ulemek was convicted in March of 1993 [sic] for the assassination of Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, by my calculations that would be eight years. I don't know what your drift is and what is the connection between me and that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, if I say 19 -- can you just answer my question. Mr. Ulemek was convicted only the 27th of May, 2007 - not 1993 as recorded - for the assassination of Mr. Djindjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly do not know how relevant this question is for the testimony of this witness generally speaking. If Mr. Harmon could explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it goes to discredit me in some way. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Relevance, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to complete the circle on this -- who this person is and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Its relevance is that this man was a paramilitary, and he was somebody who was sent to participate in this operation. It is relevant only to identify who he is and for no other purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we -- that's not the relevance we require, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We want the relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I can't establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will strike it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's go to the next man in this image, sir, the man that you have identified as Mr. Medic, the man holding the binoculars. What role did he have in the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No role, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was he doing in the trench with you and Mr. Ulemek on the 6th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, as can be seen here, he's observing his unit, some 50 men that he'd brought from the eastern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. At the time, pursuant to an order of an epidemiologist were isolated in quarantine because of an infectious disease that they contracted by using dirty water. They were kept in isolation, Madam Pajic, Dr. Pajic, epidemiologist treated them, and after they were cured they were sent packing back from where they came from. So his role and the role of his units was non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have just a minute, Your Honours, I need to consult that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Harmon, I think they called him Boca because of his first name, Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the name of the -- of his unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time there was no name, Mr. Harmon. It was a company which came from the Mirkovci Brigade, from the area of Djeletovci where it was deployed, and as such they were dispatched probably pursuant to a Main Staff of the SVK order for them to be temporarily in our composition. It bore no other name, but I do know what you're getting at now, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the unit he commanded have the name the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, that unit did not bear that name at the time. I can tell you frankly and you may or may not believe me. After the war, after Skorpions started appearing in the press, I thought I knew several units on the Croatian and Serbian side who called themselves dangerous names, Skorpions, Cobras, Bears, Wolves, et cetera, but I never heard about Skorpions, and then I was surprised six, seven years ago when I heard that Slobodan Medic's unit had been named Skorpions. You may believe me, you may not believe me, but I can't help it. At the time that unit did not bear the name Skorpions because I never heard such a name at the time anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if I can jog your memory, General. You indicated that Mr. Medic came from -- I think you said a particular area. I don't have it on the transcript anymore. But I want to submit to you that he was part of a special task unit from Belgrade. Does that refresh your recollection, sir, as to where he came from?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing could refresh my memory in the direction of what I do not know, Mr. Harmon. While I was a commander I found him in the position towards the village of Njemci as part of the Mirkovci Brigade. Whether he in the meantime changed his position or -- after I no longer was commander of the SVK is something I don't -- do not know, neither could I know anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Was the first time you met this man in -- on the 6th of April in the particular trench where you found yourselves together?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the third time in my testimony, Mr. Harmon, I repeat I saw him while I toured the 11th Corps and the positions of the Mirkovci Brigade. I cannot specify the number of that brigade. And that's -- that brigade was in the oilfields of Djeletovci and manned the front line facing the village of Nijemci. This is the third time that I repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, when you were the commander of Operation Pauk and he came toward -- and he came to participate with a unit in Operation Pauk, was this the first time - the 6th of April - that you met him? I'm talking in the context of Operation Pauk. I'm not talking in terms of the oilfields at Djeletovci.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. When he came into the composition of this group, that was the second time that I clapped my eyes on him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to show you a photograph of -- another photograph and I want you to see if you can identify this individual. It's XN398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to that photograph, what do you want to do with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't intend to seek its admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. XN398. What's the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just want to see if he can identify an individual in a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problems if the purpose is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, are you able to identify the man in the middle of the photograph wearing a moustache?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Colonel Nikola Bobic of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I've concluded my examination. I appreciate your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. On that note can we take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record show that Exhibit XN398 was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I, with the Court's permission, may re-open for a few minutes, I want to ask the witness some questions that arose as a result of his testimony at the end of the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Novakovic will be the most affected. Only briefly, because I believe we should be through with the General today. I leave it in your hands to determine that, since I have not started my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may re-open.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to focus my attention on your evidence that's found at page 25, line -- starting at line 4 when I asked you if the unit that was under the command of Mr. Medic was known as the Skorpions. And what you -- your answer was that after the war the Skorpions started appearing in the press. You went on to say: "But I never heard about the Skorpions and I was surprised six or seven years ago when I heard that Slobodan Medic's unit had been named the Skorpions. You may believe me, you may not believe me, but I can't help it. At that time that unit did not bear the name Skorpions because I never heard such a name at that time anywhere." Sir, I want to show you, if I could have XN315 on the -- as an exhibit and I want to show you a portion of this video at 18 -- 00:18:02.0?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Purpose, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To impeach the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not object it being used for impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the image that is before you at 00:18:02.0?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. I don't know what the date of the document is. I don't know its provenance and this is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the patch that's on the beret of the soldier who is in the centre of the image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if the witness is seeing this for the first time, how does he recognise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Because the image of what is on the patch is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can see it, but recognise -- I suppose you're suggesting that -- recognise from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, then let me rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you, sir, identify the patch that is on the beret of the man in the centre of the image?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this screen 18:02, the date 6th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 9 it is stated unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the witness looking at and what are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm looking at an image at 18:02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And there's no date of 6 April, 1995, on this that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't see a date either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Witness, what are you referring to when you say -- when you see a date? Perhaps you can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Novakovic, I can help by seeing the reflection in the glass. I would like to instruct Mr. Novakovic not to look at the document on one screen, but rather at the image on another screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see a photo on this left-hand screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can -- could the Court Officer please -- court usher please make sure that the witness is looking at the picture that we are all looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to identify that patch that is on the man's beret in the image that is before you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, Mr. Harmon. I've never seen a beret bearing such a patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we -- Ms. Javier, could you go to the next image, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You have another image in front of you, sir, it is at 00:18:03.0. Can you identify the patch that is on this man's beret?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, Mr. Harmon. This is part of a footage that was broadcast five or six years ago, and the images on the TV screen were unclear, making it impossible to make out the insignia or patches, and that was broadcast ten years after Operation Pauk. But I can tell you with certainty that such people did not wear such patches during the Operation Pauk. On the photograph that we discussed, Mr. Medic wore a hat, camouflage hat. This is not from that operation. What I saw on TV after the war, this refers to footage of them before they went into some other combat action. In April 1995 in the area that we discussed, those people did not wear such berets. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, the image that is on this man's beret is of a scorpion. You can see clearly a tail at the top of the image and you can see at the bottom two sets of claws. It's a scorpion, isn't it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this resembles a swan in my perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we have -- we'll go to the next image if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have -- let me just have the -- we'll go to a different item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this image be admitted for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does it impeach?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In -- it is our submission, Your Honour, that the image depicts a scorpion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may very well be, but the witness says he -- he'd never had it at the time when he was a commander. He never saw anybody wearing this at the time when he was a commander. He's not denying that this may not be a scorpion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's go to the next image, then, Your Honour, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I heard Your Honour and I accept Your Honour's point and perhaps I could defer -- I don't want to talk over Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. I'm trying to say this -- yes, we can see it's a scorpion. If this soldier wore this uniform with this patch on his head at the time of Pauk, Operation Pauk, that would impeach the witness. But if the witness says they didn't wear this kind of thing at the time, I saw it ten years after the war, how does that impeach him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I go to the next image, Your Honour, and perhaps that will enlighten us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, if we can go to XN391 and have that on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: XN315, what happens to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nothing at the moment, Your Honour. I'm not seeking its in admission at the moment, but if I could have XN391 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I guess it's still for the same purpose of impeachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not object to its being shown to the witness for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, the person in the far right of this image is you, isn't it? Did you hear my question, Witness? Is that you in the far right of this image?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that image shot during Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is the man wearing the black beret who is to your immediate right?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim unequivocally because of the blurred photo. Colonel Bulat is the person with his back to us. I can recognise him by his stature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this image be -- I'm not going to seek its admission now. I would like to play just a small portion of the video from which this was taken. It might be able to assist the witness in his identification of the man wearing the black beret. That would be XN315. If we could play that image, Your Honour -- this part of XN315.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that assist you, sir, in identifying the man wearing the beret?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that Mr. Medic, who we discussed today, was that person. But I cannot claim beyond doubt, but it's possible that it is Mr. Medic, the man we referred to today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This video, Your Honour, is at 00:51:37.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you -- does that assist you in identifying what the logo was on his beret -- on his black beret?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not assist me. I do not recall at all what was on that black beret. I'm telling you that his men either wore hats or nothing at -- on their heads. I never paid any attention to any such patches or head-gear or insignia. But absolutely I deny that anybody referred to them by that name. You won't find that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Your Honour. I just want to find another portion of this film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to defer admission on this document and just show the witness one other image. If we could play a portion of XN315, starting at 00:00:56.4, if we could play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've stopped this image at 00:01:07.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you see a man in the -- in a kind of a greenish jacket wearing a hat and his hands are in his pocket. Who is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's see if we can continue to play this and you might be able to recognise him. I want you to also pay attention to the people he is addressing in -- they're wearing black, they're in a standing formation, they have berets, and the beret has an insignia on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see these men, Mr. Harmon, and I'm certain that this photograph was not taken in the period we've been referring to or, indeed, in the place we've been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Who was the man who had his hands in his pocket and he had a green jacket on and he was addressing the men in the black? Wasn't that Mr. Medic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain because the photograph is blurred. I can only make assumptions, but I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- we'll continue to play this. It might be of assistance to you, and we'll just focus on the flag that is in the right side of this image at 00:01:27.2. You recognise what is in that image?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here in front?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There's a flag that is next to the -- between the second and third men from the right side of the image. You can see a flag with a yellowish image. Do you know what that is? Isn't that a scorpion?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is, then how come it has two heads? I'm not saying it isn't, but how can a scorpion have two tails, one going left, one right? And what does that have to do with the presence of a unit at a certain time in a certain place? I'm saying that this photograph wasn't taken in the area we've been referring to or at the time we've been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you continue, Ms. Javier, and play this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Stop the image right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is that gentleman? Are you able to identify the man in the camouflage uniform at 00:02:38.3?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the man to his left with the moustache?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a man in a camouflage uniform and one to his right, but I can't see anybody to his left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a man at the right side of the image who is to the left of the man in the camouflage uniform, and he has a moustache. Can you identify that man?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll continue to play this film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, we stopped at film at 00:04:29.6. Do you recognise these clergymen?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these clergymen in a footage that was broadcast as part of a film about the Skorpions five or six years ago on Serbian TV. I cannot confirm or deny what was said on TV then, but they were reporting about their preparations before their departure to Eastern Bosnia in the summer of 1995. That's what was said then, that they were blessed by these clergymen before their departure. That's what was said about them. I saw this on television a few years ago several times. And now you are again reproducing this footage from Serbian TV. This was said to portray their preparations before departure to Eastern Bosnia. I don't know the persons that you have just shown me nor do I know these clergymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have stopped this film at timer -- I've already indicated the timer number, so I have no further -- we're not going to view this film any further. I'm going to seek admission of these items, but not at the moment until I can lay a better foundation for them. So I've concluded my examination of this witness on this particular point and I thank you, Your Honours, for permitting me to re-open my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, once more.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope this is the last time we meet on these premises. I'm going to ask you a few questions about the topics that Mr. Harmon dealt with. I'll be very concrete and I'll try to elicit short answers. We'll see whether they will be easy too.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll try to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of August [as interpreted], at the beginning of your examination-in-chief, on the transcript page 13318, showed you extracts from a personnel file and asked you whether in that file there is a remark that at the time you were not an active-duty serviceman of the VJ, you remember. And then you said that you had shown me -- that I had shown you a document when your service in the VJ finished. Let us see Prosecution Exhibit P1783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you said on the 1st of August, did you mean to say the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Harmon began his examination on the 1st of September. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: September, not August? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, what can you say us about this document? Do you know it? Is this your signature? And what is it about?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. This document is my statement that at the time of the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of the Serbian Krajina, I do not agree to going to Serbia, to Yugoslavia, but wish to remain in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's dated 8 May 1992. We can see it on the document.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After giving the statement, were you a member of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the VJ in the sense of serving in the VJ, but I still had the status of an officer of the VJ, as a former member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on that status, did you enjoy certain status-related privileges as a member of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that context Mr. Harmon asked you, upon which you explained what you've just said, that you were no longer serving in the VJ from the moment you signed this statement. Now let me ask you a general question. What kind of relations are there in -- when you serve in a military?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're the relations of subordination, military hierarchy, and singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did these relations exist when you were in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there such relations in service under the law for those serving in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were a member of the SVK, did you have a relationship of subordination with anybody from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was in the political leadership --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Novakovic, the witness is -- I beg your pardon, the interpreter would like you to repeat your last answer, please. You said: "No, because I was in the political leadership --" and then the interpreter didn't hear the rest. What did you say. Okay. Tell us what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said the following: No, because I was subordinated to the Supreme Defence Council of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I must caution both myself and you to go a bit slower for the sake of the interpreters. We must go back to that rhythm of ours.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Perisic or his predecessor, General Zivota Panic, transfer to you or were they able to transfer to you any authority to be in -- to have a position of authority in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to a different topic. Mr. Harmon showed you a document by means of which in the year 2000 you contacted the personnel administration of the VJ and requested to be paid out the unpaid annual leave benefits for the years 1993, 1994, and 1995. My question is the following: In 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995 while you were in the war, did it matter to you to get compensation for annual leave not requested?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did -- I never even thought of taking annual leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not your officer colleagues from the SVK at that time minded not being paid benefit for annual leave not requested during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please once again repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I beg your pardon, gentlemen. Mr. Lukic and Mr. Novakovic, can you please slow down and allow each other time to answer. We understand that you speak the same language, but when one of you finishes talking, there is interpretation still taking place. Now, Mr. Novakovic, the question was: "Did you know whether or not your officer colleagues from the SVK at that time minded not being paid benefits for annual leave not requested during the war?" And then you had just started answering: "No, but they --" And then we couldn't hear what you said. Can you please repeat your answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but sometimes they requested leave to take care of some important private and family-related issues, with that leave counting against their annual leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who would they turn to to be granted this sort of leave?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each one of them would turn to their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of which army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the SVK, that's the army we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon also showed parts of the discussion at the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the VJ about what he called the Bulat case about those inquiries, as it was mentioned within the General Staff of the VJ. Let me ask you the following: We saw that statement that you signed in Banja Luka about wishing to commence service in the VJ in September 1995. Do you remember giving testimony to that effect and to what Mrksic said to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement says that I agree to be appointed to the VJ pursuant to a decision of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct. Do you know whether Mr. Bulat also made such a statement, was this something that was required of him too?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because Colonel Bulat wasn't in Banja Luka with us then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the SVK in its structure have military disciplinary courts?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was commander, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the Law on the Serbian Army of the Krajina, does it envisage the existence of military disciplinary courts, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The existence of military disciplinary courts and military criminal courts was envisaged; however, we didn't have personnel to establish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm specifically interested in military disciplinary courts, whether they were established within units or commands, but you don't know what -- how that developed once you were replaced, at least that is how I understand your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know where you get that understanding, Mr. Lukic. Nothing developed during -- when he was commander. He says he didn't have these disciplinary -- military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Now what are you talking about what developed and what replaced what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was whether the witness knew that after his replacement from the position of commander of the SVK military disciplinary courts started functioning in the SVK, that was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Phrase it that way. That's much better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When, according to you, did the SVK cease to exist as an organised army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another topic that has to do with Mr. Harmon's examination. On the same day Mr. Harmon asked you about your housing odyssey to call it that, and you said that your request for housing to be provided to you was only solved - which year was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What I would like to know is the following: You said that in the Raska garrison it was found, although you had never been there serving in the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question will be this: Do you recall when you filed your request for housing? When was it that you lodged it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I filed it in May 1992, when the JNA was withdrawing from the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the personnel centres were established or -- in other words, was the 40th Personnel Centre in function at the time when you lodged your housing request?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's broach another subject. Mr. Harmon showed you documents - now I'm referring to your examination-in-chief - concerning contacts you had with Mr. Nambiar and Mr. Goulding. He showed you UN documents, you remember, concerning their reports, focusing on the special units of police. His thesis, my learned friend's thesis, was that in those reports those units were labelled as paramilitary and that the UN was critical of them. My question to you is: Let's be precise, did you while you were commander of the 80th Brigade of special units of police, did you have immediate and personal contacts with both Mr. Nambiar and Mr. Goulding?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Nambiar, yes, directly; and with respect to contacts with Mr. Goulding, I was related of those contacts by the person who took part in those contacts and conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Zivkovic, the late Milos Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Nambiar in talking to you criticise the existence of special units of police and sought measures in respect of those?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any representative of the political leadership of the RSK relate any information to you that representatives of the UN wanted those special units of police to be disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm moving to another subject. Mr. Harmon showed you an entry from General Mladic's diary relating to the 8th of November, 1993, meeting, a meeting attended by representatives of both political and military leaderships, both of the FRY, the Republika Srpska, and Republic of Serbian Krajina. And he showed you an entry relating to the words of Minister Rakic and tried to elicit your comment, and you discussed the financial and materiel condition of the SVK at the time. That would be page 17 of LiveNote of the 31st of August [as interpreted]. You stated that you started wearing people out with your constant requests?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain who did you wear out and why did you repeat your requests time and again?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started wearing General Perisic and Mr. Milosevic out and all those representatives of Serbia's leadership, and I started wearing out the representatives of the government and leadership of the RSK. And for that reason, I stopped attending those co-ordination of tasks meetings at the General Staff of the VJ because I saw no purpose being served by my attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm moving on to another subject, but pertaining to the same portion of Mr. Harmon's cross-questioning -- cross-examination, when it came to fuel or oil, in connection with that you mentioned the Pancevo refinery. As you explained, oil products would be obtained from them on the basis of the arrangements that you explained. First of all, under whose jurisdiction was the oil refinery of Pancevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the VJ have -- hold any authority over the Pancevo oil refinery or oil industry at large?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
